questions.question: The World Happiness Report primarily relies on which type of data?

options.text: Subjective life evaluations and well-being measures

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Subjective life evaluations and well-being measures**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The World Happiness Report assesses happiness levels globally by primarily using **subjective life evaluations**, where people are asked to rate their lives on a scale, typically from 0 to 10.
 
• The report incorporates data from the **Gallup World Poll**, which collects individual responses regarding their well-being and satisfaction with life.
 
• Factors such as social support, freedom to make life choices, generosity, corruption perception, and income levels are included to provide a broader context for subjective life evaluations.
 
• Key indicators of happiness include both emotional components (positive and negative emotions) and cognitive evaluations, such as the Cantril Ladder method, where individuals rank their lives.
 
• The report’s focus on subjective measures highlights the importance of understanding how individuals perceive their own lives, rather than relying solely on objective metrics like GDP or employment rates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Objective economic indicators only**

 
 
• Objective economic indicators include metrics like GDP, employment rates, income levels, and inflation rates.
 
• While these indicators provide measurable data about a country's economy, they do not capture individuals' personal perceptions of happiness or well-being.
 
• For instance, GDP growth might not directly translate to improved happiness if wealth distribution remains unequal.
 
 
 
• **Environmental sustainability metrics**
 
 
• Environmental sustainability metrics assess factors like carbon emissions, renewable energy usage, biodiversity, and ecological footprint.
 
• Though important for sustainable development, these metrics are not directly incorporated into the World Happiness Report.
 
• However, sustainable practices indirectly contribute to societal well-being by ensuring long-term resource availability and quality of life.
 
 
 
• **Military strength and geopolitical stability**
 
 
• Military strength includes a nation’s defense capabilities, while geopolitical stability refers to political relationships and conflict resolution among nations.
 
• Though stability can impact happiness indirectly by reducing fear and promoting security, it is not a primary focus of the World Happiness Report.
 
• The report prioritizes individuals' subjective experiences over these external factors.

questions.question: The Bhakti saint who propagated devotion to Rama in the Awadhi dialect was:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tulsidas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tulsidas** was a prominent Bhakti saint and poet, known for his devotion to Lord Rama and his literary contributions in the Awadhi dialect.
 
• He is best known for authoring the **Ramcharitmanas**, a retelling of the Valmiki Ramayana in Awadhi, making it accessible to the common people of India.
 
• Tulsidas's works emphasize devotion (Bhakti) and morality, playing a significant role in popularizing the worship of Lord Rama in northern India.
 
• He was a contemporary of Emperor Akbar and lived in the 16th century, actively promoting the Bhakti movement during his time.
 
• His other notable works include **Vinaya Patrika**, **Hanuman Chalisa**, and several other devotional hymns dedicated to Lord Rama and Hanuman.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kabir**
 
 
• Kabir was a 15th-century mystic poet and saint associated with the Bhakti and Sufi movements.
 
• His compositions, known as **Dohe** (couplets), emphasize the unity of God and criticize social evils such as caste discrimination and religious hypocrisy.
 
• He did not promote devotion to any specific deity and instead focused on Nirguna Bhakti (worship of a formless God).
 
• His works are compiled in the **Bijak** and also feature in the Guru Granth Sahib.
 
 
 
• **Surdas**
 
 
• Surdas was a 16th-century Bhakti poet and saint, renowned for his devotion to Lord Krishna.
 
• He is best known for his contributions to Krishna Bhakti literature, particularly his verses in the **Sursagar**.
 
• His works focus on the childhood and playful exploits of Lord Krishna, written in Braj Bhasha.
 
• Surdas is regarded as a key figure in the Krishna Bhakti tradition.
 
 
 
• **Namdev**
 
 
• Namdev was a 13th-14th century Bhakti saint from Maharashtra, associated with the Varkari tradition.
 
• He was a devotee of Lord Vitthal (a form of Lord Krishna) and composed numerous devotional hymns in Marathi and Hindi.
 
• Namdev’s verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the holy scripture of Sikhism.
 
• His teachings emphasize devotion, equality, and the futility of ritualistic practices.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Article 312 of the Indian Constitution ?

options.text: To regulate the appointment of Supreme Court judges
To create All India Judicial Services
To determine the qualification of Members of Parliament
To define the power of the Attorney General

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To create All India Judicial Services**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 312 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to create new All India Services, including the All India Judicial Services (AIJS), in the national interest.
 
• The creation of AIJS requires a resolution to be passed by the Rajya Sabha with a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting.
 
• This provision aims to ensure uniformity and efficiency in the judicial system across the country.
 
• All India Judicial Services would function similarly to other All India Services like the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and Indian Police Service (IPS), ensuring merit-based recruitment and professional administration of justice.
 
• It is seen as a measure to improve the quality of judiciary and address the existing vacancies in subordinate courts across India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: To regulate the appointment of Supreme Court judges**
 
 
• The appointment of Supreme Court judges is governed by Articles 124 and 217 of the Constitution and follows the Collegium System, which involves the Chief Justice of India and senior judges of the Supreme Court.
 
• It is unrelated to Article 312, which focuses on the creation of All India Services.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: To determine the qualification of Members of Parliament**
 
 
• Article 84 of the Indian Constitution specifies the qualifications required for a person to become a Member of Parliament, such as age, citizenship, and other conditions.
 
• This function does not fall under the scope of Article 312, which is exclusively about creating All India Services.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: To define the power of the Attorney General**
 
 
• Article 76 of the Constitution defines the role, powers, and duties of the Attorney General of India, who is the chief legal advisor to the government.
 
• Article 312 does not deal with the Attorney General's powers or responsibilities.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: All India Services under Article 312**
 
 
• All India Services, such as the IAS and IPS, are unique administrative structures where officials serve both the Union and State governments.
 
• The creation of additional services like AIJS under Article 312 is aimed at maintaining high standards of administration and governance throughout the country.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: The Fit India Movement, promoting fitness and sports culture, was launched in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2019**__.

__
 
• The Fit India Movement was launched on **29th August 2019**, coinciding with National Sports Day in India, which commemorates the birth anniversary of hockey legend Major Dhyan Chand.
 
• It was initiated by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** as a nationwide campaign to encourage citizens to adopt healthier lifestyles and incorporate fitness into their daily routines.
 
• The movement emphasizes the importance of fitness and physical activity for all age groups and aims to address the growing concerns of lifestyle diseases in India.
 
• Under the campaign, various activities such as fitness challenges, awareness programs, and events in schools, workplaces, and communities are organized to inspire fitness and physical activity.
 
• The initiative is spearheaded by the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports** in collaboration with other government and private sector organizations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **2017**
 
 
• In 2017, there was no specific national initiative for fitness like the Fit India Movement.
 
• However, the government launched several health and wellness programs under schemes like the **Ayushman Bharat Mission**, focusing on preventive healthcare.
 
• Key developments in 2017 included the promotion of yoga and traditional systems of medicine under the Ministry of AYUSH.
 
 
 
• **2018**
 
 
• In 2018, India saw the launch of initiatives like the **Khelo India Program**, which aimed to revive sports culture in India at the grassroots level.
 
• The Khelo India Program focuses on identifying and nurturing young talent, providing them with infrastructure, and promoting a culture of sports and fitness.
 
• While Khelo India is related to fitness and sports, it is distinct from the Fit India Movement.
 
 
 
• **2020**
 
 
• By 2020, the Fit India Movement gained significant momentum with the launch of campaigns like the **Fit India School Certification** and the **Fit India Freedom Run**.
 
• The COVID-19 pandemic further highlighted the importance of fitness and immunity, leading to increased participation in fitness activities organized under the movement.
 
• However, the Fit India Movement was launched in 2019, and 2020 marked its expansion and integration with digital platforms.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme**
 
 
• The Fit India Movement is a government initiative to tackle the growing concerns of sedentary lifestyles and lifestyle-related diseases in India.
 
• It promotes activities such as walking, running, yoga, cycling, and participation in sports to build a healthier and more active society.
 
• The campaign encourages individuals, schools, workplaces, and communities to prioritize fitness and well-being as essential elements of life.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: What is the classical feature of Ashokan pillars? Greitas zivitat amestu fatuan aur 8?

options.text: They had capitals topped with lion sculptures.
They were only found in South India.
They were made of bronze and silver.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They had capitals topped with lion sculptures.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ashokan pillars are a series of monolithic stone columns built during the reign of Emperor Ashoka, who ruled the Maurya Empire from 268–232 BCE.
 
• A defining feature of these pillars is their capitals, which are often topped with sculptures of animals, most famously lions, symbolizing strength, courage, and the spread of Dharma.
 
• The most renowned example is the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, which features four lions seated back-to-back and serves as the national emblem of India today.
 
• The pillars were also inscribed with Ashoka's edicts, which communicated ethical and moral principles rooted in Buddhism.
 
• The Ashokan pillars were masterfully crafted using highly polished sandstone, showcasing exceptional Mauryan artistry and craftsmanship.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: They were only found in South India.**
 
 
• This is incorrect as Ashokan pillars were primarily located in northern and central India, including regions like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat.
 
• They were strategically placed near important trade routes, cities, and sites of Buddhist significance to ensure Ashoka's messages reached a wide audience.
 
• South India, while influenced by Ashokan policies, does not have any known Ashokan pillars.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: They were made of bronze and silver.**
 
 
• This is incorrect as Ashokan pillars were constructed from sandstone, not metals like bronze or silver.
 
• The sandstone used was often sourced from quarries in Chunar (Uttar Pradesh) or Mathura and transported to the pillar sites.
 
• The smooth polish and intricate carvings on these pillars highlight the technological advancements of the Mauryan era.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: They served as fire altars.**
 
 
• This is incorrect as the purpose of Ashokan pillars was not religious rituals involving fire but rather to disseminate the principles of Dhamma (moral law).
 
• The inscriptions on the pillars emphasized non-violence, respect for all living beings, and the promotion of social harmony.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Ashokan Pillars**
 
 
• The Ashokan pillars are among the earliest known examples of monumental stone art in India.
 
• They reflect Emperor Ashoka's adoption of Buddhism and his efforts to propagate its principles through visual and textual means.
 
• These pillars remain an enduring symbol of India's cultural and historical heritage.

questions.question: In which city is the sculptural panel of "Descent of the Ganges" located?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahabalipuram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The "Descent of the Ganges" is a famous sculptural panel located in **Mahabalipuram**, Tamil Nadu, India.
 
• It is one of the largest open-air rock reliefs in the world, measuring approximately 29 meters in length and 13 meters in height.
 
• The panel depicts the story of the sacred river Ganges descending to Earth from the heavens, as per Hindu mythology, with the help of Lord Shiva.
 
• This magnificent sculpture showcases intricate carvings of gods, demigods, animals, and other celestial beings, representing the divine event.
 
• Mahabalipuram, also known as Mamallapuram, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its group of monuments including rock-cut caves, temples, and sculptures from the Pallava period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ellora:**

 
 
• Ellora is a UNESCO World Heritage Site located in Maharashtra, India, and is famous for its rock-cut caves dating back to the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
 
• It consists of 34 caves, including Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain temples and monasteries, showcasing India's religious diversity.
 
• The most notable structure is the Kailasa Temple (Cave 16), a monolithic rock-cut temple dedicated to Lord Shiva.
 
 
 
• **Pattadakal:**
 
 
• Pattadakal, located in Karnataka, is another UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its blend of Dravidian (Southern) and Nagara (Northern) architectural styles.
 
• The site includes a group of Hindu and Jain temples from the 7th and 8th centuries, built during the reign of the Chalukya dynasty.
 
• The Virupaksha Temple and Mallikarjuna Temple are prime examples of exquisite Chalukyan architecture.
 
 
 
• **Badami:**
 
 
• Badami, also in Karnataka, is famous for its rock-cut cave temples, built during the Chalukya dynasty in the 6th and 7th centuries.
 
• The site includes four main cave temples carved into sandstone cliffs, dedicated to Hindu deities such as Shiva and Vishnu, and one Jain temple.
 
• Badami is also known for its ancient inscriptions and scenic location surrounded by hills and lakes.

questions.question: Which Nigerian author won the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2007 for "Half of a Yellow Sun"?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie** is a renowned Nigerian author known for her impactful works exploring themes of identity, feminism, and post-colonialism.
 
• She won the **Women's Prize for Fiction in 2007** for her novel "**Half of a Yellow Sun**," which is set during the Nigerian Civil War (also known as the Biafran War).
 
• "Half of a Yellow Sun" is recognized for its vivid portrayal of the war's impact on individuals and families, offering a deeply human perspective on a historical event.
 
• The Women's Prize for Fiction is a prestigious literary award recognizing outstanding fiction written by women, and Adichie's win brought significant international attention to African literature.
 
• In addition to this accolade, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie has been celebrated for other works, including "Purple Hibiscus," "Americanah," and her famous TED Talk-turned-book, "We Should All Be Feminists."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Buchi Emecheta**:
 
 
• Buchi Emecheta was a Nigerian author known for her works focusing on African women's experiences and themes of gender, migration, and identity.
 
• Her notable works include "The Joys of Motherhood," "Second-Class Citizen," and "The Bride Price."
 
• Emecheta's writing often highlights the struggles of African women in traditional and modern settings.
 
 
 
• **Lola Shoneyin**:
 
 
• Lola Shoneyin is a Nigerian poet and novelist best known for her novel "**The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives**."
 
• Her work explores polygamy, family dynamics, and societal expectations in Nigeria.
 
• Shoneyin is also the founder of the Aké Arts and Book Festival, a prominent literary event in Africa.
 
 
 
• **Sefi Atta**:
 
 
• Sefi Atta is a Nigerian author and playwright celebrated for her novel "**Everything Good Will Come**."
 
• Her works delve into themes of women's empowerment, societal challenges, and the cultural complexities of Nigeria.
 
• Atta's writing is widely acclaimed for its witty and insightful portrayal of Nigerian society.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: The Nigerian Civil War and Literature**:
 
 
• "Half of a Yellow Sun" is set during the Nigerian Civil War (1967–1970), a conflict that arose from the attempted secession of the southeastern region of Nigeria as the Republic of Biafra.
 
• The novel provides a historical narrative interwoven with personal stories, exploring the war's devastating effects on people’s lives and relationships.
 
• This theme has been a significant focus in Nigerian literature, bringing global attention to the country's history and culture.

questions.question: What is the duration of each half in a standard kabaddi match (men's)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**20 minutes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A standard kabaddi match for men consists of two halves, each lasting **20 minutes** with a 5-minute break between the halves.
 
• During the match, players aim to score points by raiding the opponent's court and tagging opponents while avoiding being caught.
 
• The total duration of a kabaddi match, including breaks, is typically **45 minutes**.
 
• Matches are conducted as per the rules set by the International Kabaddi Federation (IKF) and Asian Kabaddi Federation (AKF).
 
• Time management and stamina play a crucial role in the outcome of the match due to the high-intensity nature of the game.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 15 minutes**

 
 
• While 15 minutes is not the correct duration for a kabaddi match half, shorter game durations are often used in informal or training matches.
 
• Such durations are utilized to train players for quick strategies and improve reflexes.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: 30 minutes**
 
 
• 30 minutes refers to the total duration of a kabaddi match if both halves are combined, excluding breaks.
 
• It is sometimes confused as the length of a single half, but officially each half is 20 minutes.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: 25 minutes**
 
 
• 25 minutes is not a standard duration for kabaddi matches, though extended durations may be applied in unofficial or recreational games.
 
• Modifications in match duration are sometimes introduced in exhibition matches or non-competitive leagues for entertainment purposes.
 
 
 
• **About Kabaddi:**
 
 
• Kabaddi is a contact team sport originating from India and is widely played in South Asia.
 
• The game involves two teams of seven players each, competing to score points by raiding the opponent's side and defending their own.
 
• It has gained international recognition, with leagues such as the Pro Kabaddi League popularizing the sport worldwide.
 
• The sport emphasizes agility, strength, quick decision-making, and teamwork.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a feature of Kathakali performances?

options.text: Actors use facial expressions and hand gestures
The performance is silent with no vocalization

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The performance is silent with no vocalization**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kathakali performances are not silent;** they are accompanied by vocalization, including live singing and narration.
 
• Live singing in Kathakali is performed by vocalists who narrate the story in Malayalam, adding depth and context to the performance.
 
• The actors use intricate facial expressions, hand gestures (mudras), and body movements to depict emotions and narratives in sync with the music and vocals.
 
• The entire performance is a blend of dialogue and musical instruments, such as chenda, maddalam, and cymbals, creating a rich audio-visual experience.
 
• Silence is not a feature of Kathakali, as the vocal and instrumental components play a significant role in engaging the audience.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Masked performances:**
 
 
• While Kathakali does not involve masks, the actors use intricate makeup styles and elaborate costumes. The makeup itself serves as a mask, transforming the actors into mythological and divine characters.
 
• The makeup is categorized into types, such as Pacha (green), Kathi (knife), and Kari (black), representing different character traits like heroism, villainy, or evil.
 
 
 
• **Actors use facial expressions and hand gestures:**
 
 
• Facial expressions (Navarasas) and hand gestures (Mudras) are fundamental to Kathakali performances.
 
• These elements help narrate stories from Hindu epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana in a visually compelling manner.
 
• The facial expressions are highly exaggerated to convey emotions clearly even to distant viewers.
 
 
 
• **The performance includes live singing:**
 
 
• Live singing, known as Sopanam, is integral to Kathakali performances.
 
• Specialized vocalists sing verses in Malayalam, often adapted from classical texts, which are synchronized with the actors’ actions.
 
• The singers are accompanied by traditional instruments like chenda (drum) and maddalam, adding rhythm and intensity to the performance.

questions.question: "Raslila" is a traditional dance of which state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttar Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **"Raslila"** is a traditional dance form that originated in the Indian state of **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• It is primarily associated with the cultural and spiritual heritage of the **Braj region**, which includes Mathura, Vrindavan, and other nearby areas.
 
• The dance form depicts episodes from the life of **Lord Krishna**, particularly his childhood and youth, including his interactions with Radha and the Gopis (cowherd maidens).
 
• **Raslila** combines dance, drama, and music, making it a significant cultural expression in the region and a way to connect with the divine.
 
• This art form is performed during festivals such as **Janmashtami** (the birth of Lord Krishna) and other celebrations related to Krishna's life in temples and cultural gatherings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Punjab:**
 
 
• Punjab is known for its vibrant and energetic dance forms like **Bhangra** and **Giddha**.
 
• Bhangra is traditionally performed during the harvest festival of **Vaisakhi** and is characterized by lively music and vigorous movements.
 
• Giddha is a women-centric folk dance that involves graceful hand movements and singing boliyan (folk couplets).
 
 
 
• **Kerala:**
 
 
• Kerala is home to classical dance forms like **Kathakali** and **Mohiniyattam**.
 
• Kathakali is a highly stylized dance-drama performance known for its elaborate costumes, makeup, and storytelling through gestures.
 
• Mohiniyattam, often referred to as the "Dance of the Enchantress," is a graceful classical dance form performed by women.
 
 
 
• **West Bengal:**
 
 
• West Bengal is famous for its traditional dance forms like **Rabindra Nritya** and **Chhau dance**.
 
• Rabindra Nritya is inspired by the compositions of Rabindranath Tagore and blends Indian classical and folk dance styles.
 
• Chhau dance, originating from Purulia, is a tribal martial dance form that includes elements of storytelling, masks, and vibrant costumes.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following works was authored by Varahamihira?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Brihat Samhita**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Brihat Samhita** is an ancient Sanskrit text composed by **Varahamihira**, a renowned Indian astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer.
 
• This work is considered an encyclopedic compilation, covering diverse topics such as astronomy, astrology, geography, architecture, weather prediction, gemology, and horticulture.
 
• Varahamihira lived during the Gupta Empire and was one of the **Navaratnas** (nine jewels) in the court of King Yashodharman.
 
• The Brihat Samhita is famous for its scientific approach and practical knowledge, showcasing advanced insights into various disciplines.
 
• The text also includes chapters on planetary movements and their effects, providing valuable information that is still studied in astrology and astronomy today.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mrichchakatika**

 
 
• Mrichchakatika, also known as “The Little Clay Cart,” is an ancient Sanskrit play written by **Shudraka**.
 
• The play is a classic example of Indian drama, showcasing themes of love, political intrigue, and social justice.
 
• The central story revolves around the romantic relationship between Charudatta, a Brahmin merchant, and Vasantasena, a courtesan.
 
• It is celebrated for its realistic portrayal of human emotions and life in ancient India.
 
 
 
• **Sushruta Samhita**
 
 
• The Sushruta Samhita is one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda, attributed to **Sushruta**, an ancient Indian surgeon.

questions.question: Which system, introduced by the Government of India Act of 1919, classified provincial subjects into "reserved" and "transferred" categories?

__
 
• **Dyarchy** was introduced under the Government of India Act, 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
 
• It divided provincial subjects into two categories: **“Reserved” and “Transferred.”**
 
• The **“Reserved” subjects** were to be administered by the Governor and his Executive Council without being accountable to the legislative council. Examples include law and order, finance, and police.
 
• The **“Transferred” subjects** were administered by Indian ministers who were responsible to the legislative councils. Examples include education, public health, and agriculture.
 
• Dyarchy was an attempt to introduce **limited self-governance** in provinces by involving Indians in the administration of transferred subjects while retaining significant powers with the British authorities.
 
• This system remained in effect until it was abolished by the Government of India Act, 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• It aimed to create a federal structure by combining British Indian provinces and princely states into a single political entity.
 
• However, the federal provisions of the Act were not implemented because the princely states were not willing to join the federation.
 
 
 
• **Bicameralism**
 
 
• Bicameralism refers to a legislative system with two houses or chambers, typically an upper house and a lower house.
 
• In India, bicameralism was introduced at the central level by the Government of India Act, 1919, which established a bicameral legislature consisting of the Council of State (Upper House) and the Legislative Assembly (Lower House).
 
• Currently, India follows a bicameral system at the central level (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and in some states.
 
 
 
• **Responsible Government**
 
 
• The concept of Responsible Government implies that the executive is responsible to the legislature and ultimately to the people.
 
• In India, the principle of responsible government was fully established with the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935, made a significant move towards responsible government by introducing provincial autonomy.

questions.question: At which Lagrange point does the Aditya-L1 spacecraft orbit?

__
 
• The Aditya-L1 spacecraft is India's first dedicated solar mission and it orbits around the **Lagrange Point 1 (L1)**, located approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
 
• The L1 point is a unique location between the Earth and the Sun where the gravitational forces of both bodies and the centrifugal force of the spacecraft balance, allowing it to stay in a stable orbit.
 
• This position provides an uninterrupted view of the Sun, making it ideal for monitoring solar activities such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections.
 
• Aditya-L1 carries seven scientific payloads designed to study various aspects of the Sun, including its photosphere, chromosphere, and outermost layer, the corona.

• **L2**

• L2 is commonly used for space observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope because it provides a stable environment with minimal interference from Earth's radiation and thermal effects.
 
• At this point, the spacecraft can maintain a fixed position relative to the Earth and Sun, making it ideal for deep-space observations.
 
 
 
• **GEO (Geostationary Earth Orbit)**
 
 
• A geostationary orbit is a circular orbit approximately 35,786 kilometers above Earth's equator.
 
• Satellites in GEO appear stationary from the Earth's surface because their orbital period matches Earth's rotation period.
 
• GEO is commonly used for communication, weather monitoring, and broadcasting satellites such as GSAT and INSAT.
 
 
 
• **SSO (Sun-Synchronous Orbit)**

• Satellites in this orbit are used for Earth observation, remote sensing, and environmental monitoring due to consistent lighting conditions.
 
• Examples include satellites like India's Cartosat series for high-resolution imaging.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines population stabilization?

options.text: It refers to the stage where fertility becomes higher than mortality
It refers to zero birth rate
It occurs when the difference between birth rate and death rate is negligible
It indicates exponential growth of urban population

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It occurs when the difference between birth rate and death rate is negligible**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Population stabilization refers to the stage where the total population of a region or country stabilizes due to a negligible difference between birth rate and death rate.
 
• This occurs when the fertility rate declines to the replacement level fertility, which is approximately 2.1 children per woman.
 
• It is an essential demographic milestone that signifies a balanced population growth and plays a crucial role in sustainable development.
 
• Population stabilization leads to reduced pressure on resources such as food, water, healthcare, and infrastructure.
 
• India has been actively working towards achieving population stabilization through initiatives like the National Population Policy (2000) and programs promoting family planning and reproductive health.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: It refers to the stage where fertility becomes higher than mortality**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as higher fertility compared to mortality leads to population growth, not stabilization.
 
• Population growth occurs when the birth rate significantly exceeds the death rate, which is common in developing countries.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: It refers to zero birth rate**
 
 
• Zero birth rate implies no births are taking place, which is not population stabilization but a scenario of population decline.
 
• Population stabilization focuses on maintaining a balance, not eliminating births altogether.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: It indicates exponential growth of urban population**
 
 
• Exponential urban population growth refers to rapid migration and population increase in urban areas, leading to urbanization.
 
• This phenomenon is unrelated to population stabilization, which concerns the overall population equilibrium.
 
 
 
• **Population Stabilization: Key Terminologies**
 
 
• **Replacement Level Fertility:** The level of fertility at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, typically 2.1 children per woman.
 
• **Birth Rate:** The number of live births per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• **Death Rate:** The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• **Demographic Transition:** The process by which a country moves from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates, achieving population stabilization.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which enzyme primarily is responsible for joining "Okazaki fragments" during the DNA replication process?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**DNA ligase**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **DNA ligase** is an essential enzyme involved in DNA replication and repair processes, particularly responsible for joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
 
• Okazaki fragments are short DNA sequences synthesized on the lagging strand during replication. DNA ligase seals the gaps between these fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds.
 
• DNA ligase plays a critical role in maintaining the integrity of the DNA molecule by ensuring that the newly synthesized DNA strands are continuous and stable.
 
• This enzyme works by catalyzing the formation of a covalent bond between the 3’-hydroxyl group of one nucleotide and the 5’-phosphate group of another nucleotide.
 
• In addition to DNA replication, DNA ligase is also involved in processes such as DNA repair mechanisms, including base excision repair and double-strand break repair.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **DNA polymerase:**

 
 
• DNA polymerase is the enzyme responsible for synthesizing new strands of DNA by adding nucleotides to the 3’ end of a growing DNA strand during replication.
 
• It primarily works in a 5’ to 3’ direction and requires a primer to initiate DNA synthesis.
 
• While it synthesizes Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, it does not join them; this task is performed by DNA ligase.
 
 
 
• **Helicase:**
 
 
• Helicase is an enzyme that unwinds the double-stranded DNA molecule at the replication fork, creating two single strands that can serve as templates for replication.
 
• It breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the two strands and allowing the replication machinery to access the DNA.
 
• Helicase does not directly participate in the joining of Okazaki fragments.
 
 
 
• **Primase:**
 
 
• Primase is an RNA polymerase enzyme that synthesizes short RNA primers on the lagging strand during DNA replication.
 
• These primers provide a starting point for DNA polymerase to begin synthesizing DNA.
 
• Primase is not involved in the joining of Okazaki fragments; its role is limited to primer synthesis.
 
 
 
• **Okazaki fragments:**
 
 
• Okazaki fragments are short DNA sequences synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand during replication.
 
• These fragments are later joined together by DNA ligase to form a continuous strand.
 
• The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously because DNA synthesis can only occur in the 5’ to 3’ direction, requiring frequent initiation by RNA primers.

questions.question:
Arrange these evolutionary events chronologically:

A. First eukaryotes

B. First prokaryotes

C. Multicellularity

D. Oxygen accumulation
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1) B-D-A-C**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **B. First prokaryotes:** The earliest forms of life on Earth were prokaryotic cells, which appeared approximately 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago. These were simple, unicellular organisms without a nucleus.
 
• **D. Oxygen accumulation:** Prokaryotes, such as cyanobacteria, were responsible for the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) around 2.5 billion years ago. This event led to the accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.
 
• **A. First eukaryotes:** Eukaryotic cells, which are more complex with a defined nucleus, evolved approximately 1.8 billion years ago. This advancement allowed for more specialized cellular functions.
 
• **C. Multicellularity:** Multicellular organisms emerged around 600 million years ago, enabling the formation of complex life forms with specialized tissues and organs.
 
• The correct chronological order of these evolutionary events is **B-D-A-C:** First prokaryotes → Oxygen accumulation → First eukaryotes → Multicellularity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prokaryotes:**
 
 
• Prokaryotes are single-celled organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
 
• Bacteria and archaea are the two domains of prokaryotes.
 
• They played a crucial role in shaping early Earth's environment, including the production of oxygen through photosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **Oxygen Accumulation (Great Oxygenation Event):**
 
 
• The Great Oxygenation Event was a dramatic increase in Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels due to photosynthetic activity by cyanobacteria.
 
• This event was critical for the evolution of aerobic (oxygen-dependent) life forms.
 
• It also caused the first mass extinction by eliminating many anaerobic organisms that could not survive in oxygen-rich environments.
 
 
 
• **Eukaryotes:**
 
 
• Eukaryotic cells are characterized by a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts.
 
• The endosymbiotic theory explains their evolution, suggesting that eukaryotic cells arose through the symbiosis of different prokaryotic cells.
 
• Eukaryotes include plants, animals, fungi, and protists.
 
 
 
• **Multicellularity:**
 
 
• Multicellularity allowed organisms to develop specialized cells for different functions, such as muscle cells, nerve cells, and blood cells.
 
• This advancement led to the evolution of complex life forms, including plants and animals.
 
• Examples of early multicellular organisms include algae and simple sponges.

• It is considered an investment that contributes to the development of public assets.

• Such spending is focused on asset creation and economic development.

questions.question: Which of the folowing statements shows accurate understanding of a macroeconomic concept?

options.text: Gross Domestic Product includes earnings sent home by citizens working abroad.
When the general price level rises, the value of money tends to fall.
A country's budget is considered balanced when exports exceed imports.
The central bank controls inflation mainly through changes in income tax rates.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**When the general price level rises, the value of money tends to fall**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When the general price level in an economy rises, it leads to inflation, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
 
• This means that with the same amount of money, people can buy fewer goods and services as prices increase.
 
• The phenomenon is explained by the **inverse relationship between the value of money and price levels**: as prices increase, the value of money decreases.
 
• The value of money is often measured in terms of the quantity of goods and services it can purchase (real value).
 
• This concept is critical for understanding inflation and its effects on savings, investments, and the overall economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Gross Domestic Product includes earnings sent home by citizens working abroad.**
 
 
• This is incorrect because Gross Domestic Product (GDP) only includes the value of goods and services produced within a country’s borders.
 
• Earnings sent home by citizens working abroad are classified under **Gross National Income (GNI)** or Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA), not GDP.
 
• GDP focuses solely on domestic economic activity, regardless of who owns the production factors.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: A country's budget is considered balanced when exports exceed imports.**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as it confuses the concept of a **trade surplus** with a balanced budget.
 
• A balanced budget refers to a government’s fiscal position where its revenue equals its expenditure, not trade balances.
 
• A trade surplus occurs when a country’s exports exceed its imports, but it is unrelated to a government’s budget.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: The central bank controls inflation mainly through changes in income tax rates.**
 
 
• This is incorrect because income tax rates are determined by the government, not the central bank.
 
• The central bank primarily controls inflation through **monetary policy tools**, such as adjusting interest rates (repo rate), open market operations, and controlling the money supply.
 
• Fiscal tools like income tax rates are part of the government’s policy, not the central bank’s function.

questions.question: Trade policy prior to 1991 was characterized by
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**High tariffs and quotas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **trade policy prior to 1991 in India** was characterized by a highly restrictive and protectionist approach designed to promote domestic industries. This was done through the imposition of **high tariffs and quotas**, discouraging imports significantly.
 
• India followed a strategy of **import substitution industrialization**, wherein it aimed to reduce dependency on imported goods by encouraging domestic production.
 
• High **tariffs** were imposed on imports to make foreign goods more expensive and less competitive compared to domestically produced goods.
 
• **Quotas** were imposed, restricting the quantity of specific goods that could be imported, thereby protecting local industries from foreign competition.
 
• The **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) of 1973** further restricted the inflow of foreign capital and trade, making India’s trade regime even more closed during this period.
 
• India’s trade strategy before 1991 was also marked by the dominance of state-owned enterprises and limited engagement with the global market.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Features of India’s Pre-1991 Trade Policy:**

 
 
• The focus was on **self-reliance** and reducing dependence on foreign products.
 
• The policy promoted the development of **domestic industries** by providing them with protection from foreign competition.
 
• Foreign trade was tightly regulated by the government, and **foreign direct investment (FDI)** was minimal.
 
 
 
• **Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI):**
 
 
• This was the cornerstone of India’s trade policy before 1991, aiming to replace imported goods with domestically produced ones.
 
• Industries such as **steel, machinery, and chemicals** were promoted to achieve self-sufficiency in critical sectors.
 
 
 
• **Challenges of the Pre-1991 Trade Policy:**
 
 
• The policy led to **inefficiencies in domestic industries** due to lack of competition and innovation.
 
• India’s economic growth remained sluggish, with the average GDP growth rate being referred to as the **Hindu rate of growth** (around 3.5%).
 
• Excessive protectionism resulted in **low exports** and an unsustainable trade deficit.
 
 
 
• **Post-1991 Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• The **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) reforms** marked a significant shift in India’s trade policy, moving towards a more open and market-driven economy.
 
• **Tariffs were lowered**, quotas were abolished, and FDI policies were liberalized to integrate India into the global economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Tariffs:** Tariffs refer to taxes imposed on imported goods. In pre-1991 India, tariffs were extremely high, making imports prohibitively expensive.
 
• **Quotas:** Quotas are quantitative restrictions on imports. India used quotas extensively to limit the availability of foreign goods in the domestic market.
 
• **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA):** Enacted in 1973, this act regulated foreign investments and foreign exchange transactions, further limiting trade and investment inflows.
 
• **Protectionist Policies:** These policies were implemented to encourage the growth of domestic industries but often led to inefficiencies and lack of competitiveness.
